chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Logic of Mean Reversion

lessons.title: Random Walks, Stationarity, and Why Not Everything Reverts

children.text: The Sensex today sits at many multiples of where it stood twenty years ago. Nobody sensible is waiting for it to "revert" to its 2005 level. Yet a single NSE-listed stock's price relative to its own 20-day moving average snaps back, again and again, month after month. Same asset class, two completely different statistical behaviors happening at the same time, on the same exchange. The first two lessons of this course showed you what mean reversion looks like and how it differs from momentum. This lesson gives you the piece underneath both: why some things have a level to come back to at all, and why some genuinely do not.

body.text: A random walk has no memory and no fixed level to return to. Each step is unpredictable given the last, so after enough steps the process can be almost anywhere. A stationary series, by contrast, fluctuates around a fixed (or slowly evolving) mean with roughly constant variance, which is exactly what gives it something to revert to. Most raw asset prices behave like random walks with drift. What actually reverts, in practice, is a specific, deliberately constructed deviation from a reference point, never the raw price series itself.

children.text: The Random Walk: No Memory, No Anchor

markDefs.definition: The proposition that current prices already reflect all information contained in past prices, so tomorrow's price change cannot be predicted from today's price history alone.

children.text: A random walk is a process where each step is independent of the last: heads, you go up by a fixed amount, tails, you go down, with a fair coin deciding each new step regardless of how many heads or tails came before. Flip that coin ten thousand times and plot your running total. The path wanders. It does not politely return to zero, because nothing in the process is pulling it back there. This is close to how the weak form of the

describes short-term price changes in a liquid, well-covered stock: today's move is close to unpredictable from yesterday's move alone. Add a small, steady upward push to every step, representing earnings growth, retained profits, and inflation compounding year after year, and you get a random walk with drift, which is a reasonable rough description of a long-run, well-diversified index like the Nifty 50 or the Sensex. It wanders unpredictably in the short run, but it drifts upward on average over decades. Neither behavior involves reverting to an old level.

body.title: A random walk vs a stationary series over 200 steps (illustrative simulation)

body.text: Look at the two lines at step 200. The random walk has drifted well away from its starting point of 100, with no tendency to come back, each new excursion just builds on the last. The stationary series is still oscillating around 100, exactly as it was at step 0. Neither line "knows" where it is going next in the short run, but only one of them has a home to return to.

children.text: Stationarity: The Property That Makes Reversion Possible

A series is stationary, informally, when its statistical personality does not change over time: the average level, the typical size of swings around that average, and how today's value relates to yesterday's all look roughly the same whether you examine January to June or July to December. A stationary series has a home. It can wander away from that home for a while, but the pull back toward it is baked into the process itself. This is the actual mathematical requirement behind everything in this course. A raw stock price is almost never stationary, a growing company's fair value should genuinely rise over time, so there is no fixed level for the price to keep returning to. What is often stationary, or close enough to trade as such, is a specifically constructed deviation: the gap between a price and its own rolling moving average, the gap between a company's current valuation multiple and its own trailing five-year average, or the spread between two fundamentally linked stocks. You never trade mean reversion on a raw price level. You trade it on a deliberately built, stationary-ish deviation from a defined reference point.

content.caption: A random walk: today's price equals yesterday's price plus an unpredictable shock. There is no term pulling P_t back toward any fixed level.
A stationary, mean-reverting process (AR(1)): each step pulls the deviation from the mean back in by a fraction (1 minus phi). Chapter 2 uses this exact form to derive the half-life of a reversion.

children.text: The entire difference between the two equations is that second term, the pull back toward mu. In the random walk, it is missing entirely. In the mean-reverting process, phi controls how strongly the series is pulled home: closer to 0, and it snaps back fast, closer to 1, and it drifts for a long time before returning. If phi is greater than or equal to 1, the process stops being stationary altogether. This single number, sometimes described by saying the series "has a unit root" when it is missing this pull entirely, is what the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test formally checks for. This course keeps the mechanics of that formal test out of scope, and Chapter 2 instead builds the practical, intuition-level tools, the z-score, autocorrelation, and half-life, that you need to trade single-asset reversion without running a hypothesis test first. The full ADF and Engle-Granger testing procedure, applied to spreads between two stocks, is covered start to finish in the Introduction to Statistical Arbitrage course.

There are three distinct ways a price series can fail to be stationary, and each one breaks mean reversion in a different way. The first is structural growth: a genuinely improving business, like the Titan and Asian Paints examples from Lesson 2, has a mean that is itself rising, so the price never reverts to an old, lower level because that old level is not the true mean anymore, it is just history. The second is structural decline: a business that is genuinely deteriorating has a mean that is falling, and in the worst cases heading toward zero, so "it's cheap relative to its five-year average" is not a reversion signal, it is a lagging description of a falling process. The third, and the most dangerous for a reversion trader, is a one-time structural break, a sudden, permanent shift in the mean itself, triggered by something like a change in promoter holding, a regulatory shift, or the loss of a dominant client, after which the old mean is simply the wrong number to revert to, even though the price series looked perfectly well-behaved right up until the break.

body.label: A simple gut-check for stationarity
body.value: Does it look the same in any 6-month window?
body.context: If the average level and the size of the swings around it look roughly similar whichever 6-month window you pick, treat the series as plausibly stationary. If the average itself keeps climbing, falling, or jumping between windows, it is not, and reversion tools will mislead you.

body.title: Is a flat five-year price proof of reversion?
body.scenario: A friend points out that a mid-sized IT services stock is trading today at almost exactly the same price it traded at five years ago. "See," he says, "that's mean reversion in action, it always comes back to where it started."
body.prompt: Is a price returning to an old level, on its own, evidence that the stock is mean-reverting? What else could explain this?
body.modelAnswer: No. A price ending up near an old level is not, by itself, evidence of a mean-reverting process. A pure random walk can easily wander back near its starting point purely by chance, that tells you nothing about whether it is predictably pulled there. It is equally consistent with a business whose fundamentals have genuinely stagnated for five years, in which case the flat price reflects flat earnings power, not a statistical pull toward a mean. Real evidence of mean reversion requires showing that deviations from a defined reference point are repeatedly and reliably corrected, not pointing at one coincidental round trip.

body.title: Spotting the non-stationary case
body.question: Which of the following price behaviors is the clearest example of a structural break that invalidates the old mean, rather than a normal, tradeable overreaction?
options: A stock falls 10% on a weak quarter and recovers over the next month as the market digests a fuller picture
A stock's largest client, representing 40% of revenue, publicly terminates its contract, and the stock re-rates permanently lower
A stock's price oscillates within a ₹200 range for six months with no major news
A stock rises 3% on a day the Nifty rises 3%, with no stock-specific news
body.explanation: The loss of a client representing 40% of revenue is a genuine, permanent change to the company's earnings power. The old average price was built on a fundamental reality that no longer exists, so there is no reason for the price to revert to it. The other options describe a normal overreaction (A), a stable, likely stationary range (C), and ordinary market-wide beta (D), none of which involve the mean itself shifting.

body.title: Random Walks and Stationarity: Core Terms

cards.definition: A process in which each step is independent of the previous one, so the series has no fixed level to return to and can drift arbitrarily far from any starting point.
The property of a series whose mean, variance, and autocorrelation structure stay roughly constant over time, giving it a stable level to revert to when it deviates.
A small, steady directional push added to a random walk at each step, such as the long-run upward drift in a broad, growing stock index.

The technical property a series has when it behaves like a random walk rather than a stationary process, informally, when there is no force pulling it back to a fixed mean. Formally tested using the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test.
A sudden, permanent shift in a series' true mean, after which its historical average is no longer the correct level to expect a reversion toward.

points: A random walk has no memory and no fixed level to return to, each step is unpredictable given the last, so the series can drift arbitrarily far over time.
A stationary series has a roughly constant mean and variance over time, which is exactly what allows deviations from that mean to be reliably expected to correct.

Raw asset prices are almost never stationary. What actually reverts, in every strategy this course covers, is a deliberately constructed deviation from a defined reference point, not the raw price itself.

Not everything reverts for three distinct reasons: structural growth (the mean is genuinely rising), structural decline (the mean is genuinely falling), and structural breaks (the mean has permanently shifted).

A price returning to an old level once is not proof of mean reversion. Proving reversion requires showing that deviations are repeatedly and reliably corrected, which Chapter 2 gives you the tools to actually measure.
